**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Say what a scraper and an API each are and when either is the wrong answer, and name your own data source, its access route, its timeline and your plan B — including whether you need IRB approval or a data-use agreement before January.

## Before class

**Reading.** TBD

The opening quiz is on this reading.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

First, code — not how to write it, but what it is and why you cannot avoid understanding it. What a language actually is and why there are several: R grew out of statistics, Python out of general programming, Stata out of applied economics, and SQL is not really the same kind of thing at all. Why every serious analysis is code whether or not you wrote it, why a spreadsheet stops being enough at exactly the point your project gets interesting, and the argument that matters here — code is the only version of an analysis that can be checked, repeated, and handed to somebody else. You will drive it through an assistant, but you cannot check what you cannot read at all. Then the landscape of sources: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels — what each costs in money and in months, starting with what Cornell already pays for. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long, what they forbid you from publishing. Ethics and the IRB in brief, with the detail on the resources page. Then scraping and APIs: what each is, what it can and cannot get you, and what the terms of service and the law actually say

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

A scrape, run live from the front, and then broken on purpose. We pull a table off a page, and then watch every way it fails: the page changes and the code returns nothing, the rate limit bites, records are missing and nothing tells you, the terms of service say no, and there is no version of what you pulled that anybody could reproduce next week. Then the same data through a proper API, and then the same data simply downloaded — usually faster than either. The lesson is not that scraping is bad, it is that it is the last resort dressed up as the clever one. Then the acquisition clinic on your own project: which source exactly, what route, how long, what it costs, what plan B is. Your memo outline — six topic sentences — is written from that, and it is due before the weekend

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.
